claims.statement: APIHandler.CreateExecution (POST /{action}/run) validates the action exists in the catalog, decodes the request body into openapi.ExecutionRequest, builds a models.Execution via models.ExecutionFromRequest with status 'pending', persists it with store.CreateExecution, and returns 202 Accepted with a HAL self-link to GET /runs/{id} — it never calls the executor synchronously.

After persisting a new execution, APIHandler calls notifier.Notify() (satisfied by worker.Pool via the ExecutionNotifier interface) to wake a worker immediately instead of waiting for the next poll interval.

worker.Pool runs a configurable number of goroutines that each loop calling store.ClaimNextExecution; when nothing is pending they block on either the pool's Notify channel or a pollInterval ticker, so correctness never depends on a notify actually arriving.

ClaimNextExecution atomically selects the oldest pending execution and transitions it to 'running' inside one transaction; SQLiteStore relies on a single serialized connection while PostgresStore uses SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so concurrent workers/replicas never claim the same row.

worker.Pool.New clamps concurrency to at least 1 and a non-positive pollInterval to a 5s default; production defaults are WorkerConcurrency=4, WorkerPollInterval=5s, WorkerExecutionTimeout=2m, each overridable via ROSA_TA_WORKER_CONCURRENCY / ROSA_TA_WORKER_POLL_INTERVAL / ROSA_TA_WORKER_EXECUTION_TIMEOUT.

Pool.process maps a Runner's RunResult to a terminal status, converts the action result via models.OutputFromActionResult (forcing status to 'failed' on conversion error), and persists it with store.UpdateExecutionWithResult using a context detached from cancellation (context.WithoutCancel) but bounded by its own timeout, so a shutdown-time cancellation cannot leave an execution stuck at 'running'.

The failure reason (RunResult.Reason) is only surfaced via structured logging today; neither the executions table nor the generated openapi.Execution type has a column/field to persist or return it to API callers.

On SIGINT/SIGTERM, cmd/server cancels the worker pool's context, gives the HTTP server up to 30s to drain, then waits up to the remainder of that same 30s window for in-flight worker executions (Pool.Wait) before exiting, warning if that wait times out.

models.Execution persists status as one of the openapi.ExecutionStatus values (pending, running, succeeded, failed, timed_out), but only pending/running/succeeded/failed are ever written by the current pipeline; no code path sets timed_out, since a worker execution timeout surfaces as an executor error and is mapped to 'failed' like any other error.

ExecutorRunner.Run resolves the persisted action name via actions.CreateAction and decodes the persisted JSON params back into map[string]string, runs Executor.Execute under a per-execution timeout context, and always calls Execute with Target left nil so the resolved Scope derives the target from params.

ExecutorRunner.Run distinguishes a result.Error (which includes both genuine action failures and target-derivation failures that never reached authorization) from a result.Error==nil && !result.Allowed denial, but both are mapped to the same worker-level 'failed' execution status since the OpenAPI ExecutionStatus enum has no distinct 'denied' state.

Executor.Execute builds an audit.Record and logs it via a deferred call registered before any scope resolution, target derivation, authorization, or run logic executes, guaranteeing exactly one audit entry per execution regardless of outcome.

Executor.Execute treats three terminal states as distinct and audits each differently: no scope configured or authorization denial (DecisionDenied/OutcomeSkipped, Result.Allowed=false, no Error), target-derivation failure before authorization ran (OutcomeFailure, Result.Error set, Allowed left false, explicitly not reported as a denial), and a post-authorization Scope.Run failure (OutcomeFailure with the audited cause, Result.Allowed=true but Error set).

executor.Failure separates a caller-facing Message from an underlying Cause; Executor.auditedCause unwraps a *Failure via errors.As and records Cause (not the Failure's combined Error() string) in the audit trail, so the audited cause stays independent of a scope's caller-facing wording, while Cause is optional and Error() falls back to Message alone when nil.

executor.Scope is the interface boundary that keeps Executor domain-agnostic (Supports, DeriveTarget, Authorize, Run); its doc comment states a new scope cannot be added without separately deciding how it authorizes, and Executor.scopeFor dispatches to the first registered scope whose Supports(action) returns true.

KubeScope and AWSScope are both implemented and both registered with the executor in cmd/server/main.go and cmd/action-cli/main.go; AWS is not an unimplemented or undecided extension point but a working second scope with its own authorization story.

KubeScope.DeriveTarget builds an actions.ResourceTarget purely from caller-supplied params and always sets ClusterScoped to false, deliberately never inferring cluster-scoping from an absent namespace, because doing so previously let a caller bypass the namespace allowlist entirely.

KubeScope.Run requests a Backplane session scoped to exactly the RBAC rules the action's RequiredRBAC(target) declares (plus a pod executor when the action's UsesPodExec() is true), giving each primitive action its own least-privilege session rather than reusing one standing session.

AWSScope.DeriveTarget always resolves the AWS region from the target cluster itself via the AWS client provider's DefaultRegion lookup rather than from caller-supplied params, and for AWSWriteAction actions additionally refuses a caller-supplied resource param that disagrees with what the write action actually acts on and resolves the cluster's infrastructure ID from OCM for an ownership check.

AWSScope.Authorize checks the resolved region against a region allowlist and, for write actions, the action's self-declared Operation() against a separately configured operation allowlist; both AWS allowlists (AllowedRegions and AllowedOperations) default to empty, so an unconfigured deployment can neither read nor write any AWS resource.

catalog.ActionDefinition declares three write-safety metadata fields — DryRunAction, WriteCooldownSeconds, and Approval — surfaced via GET /{action}, but no action registered in catalog.New() sets any of them, and no code in the worker, executor, or either scope reads or enforces them; docs/adding-a-trusted-action.md explicitly states there is no approval enforcement system today.

GET /runs/{id} returns execution metadata and separately probes store.GetExecutionOutput only to decide whether to attach an output HAL link, without inlining the output; GET /runs/{exec_id}/output returns the persisted ExecutionOutput (Message plus a Resources list that is always serialized as an empty list rather than null) once a run reaches a terminal status.

The rta CLI (cmd/rta main + internal/rta.NewCommand) is purely an HTTP client of the Trusted Actions API: rta action list/describe call GET / and GET /{action} for discovery, and rta action run builds an openapi.ExecutionRequest from --cluster/--jira/--param/--dry-run/--force flags and calls Client.CreateExecution, a plain POST /{action}/run with no client-side authorization or validation beyond flag parsing.

rta action run without --no-wait calls waitForCompletion, which polls Client.GetExecution (GET /runs/{id}) on a 2-second ticker until the execution reaches a terminal status (succeeded, failed, or timed_out) or the command's --timeout (default 5 minutes) elapses, then fetches Client.GetExecutionOutput (GET /runs/{exec_id}/output) to print the result; --no-wait instead prints the 202-accepted pending Execution immediately.

internal/rta.Client prefixes every request with /api/v0/trusted-actions, resolves its bearer token from --token or an OCM CLI config file's access token (refusing to proceed if the OCM token is missing, empty, or expired), refuses to send a token over a non-HTTPS/non-loopback server URL, and rejects any redirect that would downgrade an HTTPS connection to plain HTTP.

A non-2xx response from the Trusted Actions API is decoded by internal/rta.Client into an *APIError carrying the request method/path, HTTP status code, and the server's structured code/reason from openapi.Error when present (falling back to a truncated raw response body), so rta surfaces the same denial/failure reasons the server produced rather than a generic HTTP error.

cmd/action-cli remains a separate, standalone test CLI that does not call the HTTP API at all: it wires up the same internal/executor.Executor, authorization, audit, and backplane/AWS client machinery in-process to run one primitive action directly against a cluster via kubeconfig, bypassing the server, worker pool, and store entirely.
